title: The Lamb Holds the Scroll
description: Revelation 6, 16 and 19 show the slain Lamb holding history, God patient but not indifferent, and the King returning. Why the end calls for watchmen, not panic.
body:
Root Scripture (KJV): Revelation 5:1–10; 6:1; 16:1; 19:11, 14–16 · Companion: Revelation 14:1

There are two easy ways to read the Book of Revelation, and both are wrong.

The first is to read it like a war map pinned to this week's headlines — circling dates, matching every earthquake and election to a seal or a vial, and living in a low hum of dread. The second is to close it because it is strange, violent, and hard to follow, and decide it has nothing to say to an ordinary Tuesday.

A soldier on watch can't afford either mistake. He doesn't panic at every sound in the dark, and he doesn't fall asleep at his post. He knows two things: who is in command, and what his own job is tonight.

Revelation gives us both.

## Before the Seals: A Lamb

Before a single seal breaks, John is shown a sealed book in the right hand of Him who sits on the throne — and a problem: "no man in heaven, nor in earth, neither under the earth, was able to open the book" (Revelation 5:3). John weeps.

Then an elder says, "Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book" (5:5). John turns to see a lion — and sees instead "a Lamb as it had been slain" (5:6).

That is the hinge of everything that follows. The One with authority over history is not a distant force. He is the crucified and risen Christ, still bearing the marks of the cross. Heaven's song makes the connection plain: "Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood" (5:9).

## I. The Scroll Is Opened

"And I saw when the Lamb opened one of the seals, and I heard, as it were the noise of thunder, one of the four beasts saying, Come and see." — Revelation 6:1

(A word note: the KJV's "beasts" here translates a Greek word meaning "living creatures" — the worshiping beings around the throne in Revelation 4, not the beast of Revelation 13.)

Notice who acts. The Lamb opens. What follows in chapter 6 is hard — conquest, war, scarcity, death, martyrdom, the shaking of heaven and earth. But none of it breaks loose behind His back. History is not unraveling outside of God's control. Every page turns under the hand that was pierced for sinners.

The chapter ends with people of every rank hiding in the rocks, begging to be hidden "from the wrath of the Lamb: For the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand?" (6:16–17).

It's the right question, and chapter 7 answers it. John sees "a great multitude, which no man could number … stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes" (7:9). Who are they? "These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb" (7:14).

Who shall be able to stand? Not the strong. Not the most prepared. The washed.

## II. The Vials Are Poured Out

"And I heard a great voice out of the temple saying to the seven angels, Go your ways, and pour out the vials of the wrath of God upon the earth." — Revelation 16:1

The KJV's "vials" are shallow bowls. Revelation 15:1 says that in these last plagues "is filled up the wrath of God." This is judgment reaching its appointed fullness. The angel of the waters calls it just: "Thou art righteous, O Lord … because thou hast judged thus" (16:5).

Here is what we must not miss: God's patience is not indifference. "The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance" (2 Peter 3:9). His delay of judgment is room to repent.

And yet, under the vials, the record is grim. People "blasphemed the name of God … and they repented not to give him glory" (16:9; see also 16:11). Under these judgments, their refusal to repent is exposed: they blaspheme God rather than give Him glory.

Then, right in the middle of the bowls, Jesus Himself breaks in: "Behold, I come as a thief. Blessed is he that watcheth, and keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked, and they see his shame" (16:15).

That is the watch order — given in the middle of the storm.

## III. The King Returns

"And I saw heaven opened, and behold a white horse; and he that sat upon him was called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he doth judge and make war. … And the armies which were in heaven followed him upon white horses, clothed in fine linen, white and clean. And out of his mouth goeth a sharp sword, that with it he should smite the nations … And he hath on his vesture and on his thigh a name written, KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS." — Revelation 19:11, 14–16

He came once as the suffering Servant who stood silent before Pilate. He returns as the King before whom every ruler must answer. His robe is "dipped in blood," and "his name is called The Word of God" (19:13).

Look closely at the battle. The armies follow Him in clean white linen — and the text never says they strike a blow. The only weapon named is the sword that comes out of His mouth (19:15, 21). This is not a desperate fight with an uncertain end. The gathered opposition cannot withstand the rightful King.

A Note on the 144,000

Revelation 14:1 gives a companion scene: "And I looked, and, lo, a Lamb stood on the mount Sion, and with him an hundred forty and four thousand, having his Father's name written in their foreheads."

Revelation does not say the 144,000 ride with Christ in the chapter 19 battle — these are related but separate visions. Christians also disagree about who the 144,000 are, and this piece won't settle that. But the text tells us plainly what marks them: "These are they which follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth," and "in their mouth was found no guile" (14:4–5). Following, and truth-telling. Every believer can learn from that picture.

Christians also read the timing of Revelation's visions in different ways. What every faithful reading shares is what this piece rests on: Christ rules history, judgment is real, His return is certain, and the call to respond is now.

Standing Your Watch Today

So what does a watchman do with Revelation?

He doesn't panic. The scroll is in the right hands, and those hands have nail scars.

He doesn't shrug. God's patience is mercy with a purpose. If there's something you've been putting off — a sin to confess, a return to God you keep delaying — the open door is today.

He doesn't pick up the King's sword. When evil makes us want to see someone get what's coming, Revelation shows a better way. Even the martyrs under the altar, with every reason to want justice, bring their cry to God — "How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood" (6:10) — and are told to rest (6:11). "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Romans 12:19). The sword belongs in His mouth, not our hands.

He follows, and he tells the truth. The people with the Lamb are known by where they walk and what comes out of their mouths.

And if the question "who shall be able to stand?" makes you afraid — that's an honest question. But the answer is not your record. It's robes washed in the blood of the Lamb. The last chapter of Revelation still says: "And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely" (22:17).

Come while the door is open. Then stand your watch.

## 2. Prayer

Lord Jesus, Lamb of God,

You alone were worthy to take the book and open it.

You were slain, and by Your blood You redeemed us to God.

The world feels loud and loose today, but it is not out of Your hands.

Forgive me for the times I mistook Your patience for Your absence

and put off what You plainly told me to do.

Forgive me for wanting to hold the sword that belongs to You alone.

Thank You that the question, "Who shall be able to stand?" has an answer —

and that the answer is Your blood, not my record.

Keep me awake. Help me keep my garments clean.

Put truth in my mouth, and no guile.

Teach me to follow You wherever You go.

And give me courage to say to someone today, "Come."

Faithful and True, King of kings and Lord of lords,

Thy kingdom come.

Amen.

## 3. Field Order — Hold Your Post

OBJECTIVE: Stand today as a watchman who trusts the Lamb — not a panicked spectator, not a sleeping sentry.

SITUATION: The world's noise will tell you things are out of control. Your own heart may tell you to delay repentance, or to want revenge.

ACTIONS:

1. Read Revelation 5:1–10 aloud once. Then say out loud who holds the scroll.

2. Name one thing God has plainly told you to do that you've been delaying. Take the first step today.

3. If anger at someone rises, pray Romans 12:19 and hand that person to God by name.

4. Speak only what is true today. If you shade the truth, correct it the same day.

5. Pass on the invitation to one person: "whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely" (Revelation 22:17).

IF–THEN CUE: When the headlines make it feel like the world is coming apart, then I will remember who holds the scroll, pray "Thy kingdom come," and do the next faithful thing in front of me.

GRACE BOUNDARY: You stand by the blood of the Lamb, not by finishing this list. These exercises are helps, not a measure of your standing before God. If you sin, confess it. If you miss an exercise, resume without treating the missed task as a spiritual debt. If fear about the end times is crowding out sleep or daily life, talk with your pastor or a trusted believer — and a counselor if you need one.

FRUIT CHECK (tonight): Did I bring my fear to God in prayer and take a faithful step? Did I take one obedient step I'd been putting off? Did I hand someone to God instead of nursing revenge? Did I tell the truth?
